episode_title: Tracing the history of a wooden boat

segments.text: Welcome to Workbench Conversations. The original shipyard ledger dates this hull to 1924. The next owner replaced its keel after a storm. Look at the old fastener holes along the planks; they show how that repair was carried out.
We will get back to the ledger in a minute, but first let me do our sponsor read.
Yes, go ahead. Wait, can you hear that drilling outside? Let me move this microphone.
That is much better. Somebody has also left a giant coffee cup in front of my script. It has a tiny anchor painted on it. Very appropriate. All right, where was I?
Our sponsor today is HarborSafe insurance. Restoring an old boat takes time, and the right coverage helps you protect that work.
I wanted a policy that understood vintage boats and the tools I keep aboard. Their team helped me understand my options without rushing me.
Visit harborsafe.example slash workbench for a quote. Thanks to HarborSafe for supporting this show.
Now, the next entry in the ledger is important. The yard replaced the port-side frame but left the starboard side intact. You can still see the difference in the grain.

For next week's reporting, we are looking for people who worked at this shipyard. If that is you, please send us a voice memo describing what the yard was like. Your memories will help us fill a gap in the historical record.

Returning to the keel repair, the bolts tell a different story from the invoice. They were replaced twice, not once. The first set rusted, while the second set is still intact. This is why we compare written records with the evidence in the boat itself.
That is our investigation for today. Research by Mara and sound editing by Ellis.
